t: He stole and has nothing with which to pay the principal. He has no money to pay the value of what was stolen (but if he has no money to pay the fine, he is not sold).
As we explained in Hilchot Genevah. 3:11-17.
In Deuteronomy. The book of Deuteronomy.
"And if your brother becomes poor". If he becomes destitute and poor.
And he may not sell himself and set aside the money. He may not sell himself in order to save the money he will receive.
Unless he needs it only for food. He may sell himself only in order to buy food to sustain his body.
Clothing. A garment.
We already explained. Hilchot Genevah 3:12.
And she does not acquire a slave. From the age of nine and up; but a minor slave, or a maidservant even if grown, may acquire (below 9:6).
Because of suspicion. Lest she commit adultery with him.

"And he shall return to his family" - one who has a family. The verse says that a Hebrew slave returns to his family in the Jubilee year, and from this the Sages learned that only one who has a family is sold as a Hebrew slave, excluding a convert, whose family ties are severed at the time of conversion.
He may not sell himself to a gentile. Lest he learn from his evil deeds.

Or to the stock of a convert's family - to the stock of this one who is sold to idolatry. Idolatry is called "stock" (eker) in the verse because it must be uprooted (ekor) from the world (Ramban, Leviticus 25:47).
You do not need him. You are not obligated to prevent him.
It is a mitzvah to redeem him. See also below 2:7, Hilchot Matnot Aniyim 8:13.
Publicly upon the stone of sale. In public upon the large stone on which slaves are placed for sale.
In an alley. In the street.
It is forbidden to work any Hebrew slave with rigor. For the law of rigorous labor with a Canaanite slave see below 9:8.
Work that has no limit. That has no bound or fixed measure.
To cool for him. To chill, to cool.
And likewise a gentile to whom he was sold. A gentile who bought an Israelite as a slave.
He treats him only as a hired worker. He treats him like a craftsman he hired for a particular job.
A bathhouse attendant for the public. Responsible for operating a bathhouse.
A baker. One who bakes.
His master. His owner.
He should not teach him any trade at the outset. He should not teach him a new trade that he did not practice before he was sold.
He is enslaved to the one who paid the tax for him. To the person who paid the tax in his place (see also Hilchot Gezelah 5:16).
It is permitted to use him more than enough. Even more than the amount of the tax he paid for him, and there is no interest involved in this (Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 5:17).
But not as a slave. Because they are enslaved against their will, and their law is that of a Hebrew slave and not a hired worker.
And in lodging. Living quarters.
Kibar bread. Bread made of coarse flour that was not sifted sufficiently.
Wool pieces. Pieces of wool.
You live in the city and he lives in a village, or you in a village and he in the city. For there is an advantage to living in a large city and an advantage to living in a village.

As it says, "and he shall go out from you". The verse is precise in its wording: when the slave is freed he does not go out from under you but from "with you" - from being equal to you, for during servitude he is equal to you (Alshich, Leviticus 25:41).
Whoever buys a Hebrew slave is like one who acquires a master for himself. For he must provide for all his needs as he provides for himself and his family.
As it says, "and over your brothers the children of Israel, a man over his brother". The continuation of the verse: "you shall not rule over him with rigor."
And we already explained. Hilchot Shemitah VeYovel 10:8.
That the court sold him. To pay for his theft (above 1:1).
Acquired with money. He becomes acquired by the master through the master paying his price.
And with the equivalent of money. Something that has monetary value.
Six years from the day of his sale. Full years, from the day he was sold until that same day six years later (Tosefta Parah 1:7, Bavli Arachin 18b).
As it says, "in this Jubilee year". The continuation of the verse: "you shall return, each man to his holding."
He may sell himself for more than six. He is permitted to sell himself for more than six years.
Or he suffered intermittent illnesses. Non-consecutive periods.

If the total is less than four years, they count for him toward the six etc.. A slave is acquired by his master in bodily acquisition, and therefore it is the master who loses from the slave's illness. But all this is where the slave worked at least three years, for the verse (Leviticus 25:40) equated him to a hired worker, and regarding a hired worker it says (Isaiah 16:14), "in three years, like the years of a hired worker." And since part of a year counts as a year, if he was ill less than four years, it turns out that he worked two years and a bit, which count as three years, and he need not make up. But if he was ill longer than that, he must make up all the days of illness (Aruch HaShulchan HeAtid, Zera'im 41:15-16, based on Tosafot Kiddushin 17a).
To do needlework. To sew clothing.
If he was not redeemed. For the ways of his redemption see the next halacha.
He goes out only in the Jubilee. Or upon the master's death (below, halacha 12).
If his means do not suffice. He has no money of his own.
And the nearest relative comes first. The obligation falls upon the closest relatives, and if they are unable, the obligation passes to more distant relatives.

As it says, "or his uncle or his uncle's son shall redeem him" etc.. The previous verse says, "one of his brothers shall redeem him," and afterward it says, "or his uncle or his uncle's son shall redeem him, or any close relative of his family shall redeem him," so a brother comes before an uncle, an uncle before an uncle's son, and an uncle's son before more distant relatives.
Whether relatives redeemed him or another person redeemed him, he goes out to freedom. For he does not need to work for the redeemer for the value of the redemption money, but is completely freed.
And he may redeem in parts. He is permitted to pay part of the price of his sale and reduce the years of his servitude.
The relatives do not redeem him. They are not obligated to redeem him (Kesef Mishneh).
To give according to the remaining years. To give the required amount according to the years he has left to work, as explained in the next halacha.
If they sold him for sixty dinars. And since a sale by the court is for six years, each year of work is worth ten dinars.
And he found the means. He obtained money.
And ten years remained until the Jubilee at the time of sale. He was sold to a gentile ten years before the Jubilee, so each year of work is worth ten dinars.

He is redeemed from the gentile with money and not with the equivalent of money. Although generally the equivalent of money has the law of money, there is a special teaching regarding redemption from a gentile that he is redeemed with money only (Yerushalmi Kiddushin 1:2).
And he became healthy and his value increased. He grew strong and improved and his value as a slave rose.
He became ill and his value decreased. He weakened and his value as a slave fell.
As we explained. Above, halacha 7.

Sometimes it will be to be lenient and sometimes to be stringent. For he must always pay according to his current value, and the fact that he is permitted to redeem in parts will sometimes be to his benefit and sometimes to his detriment.
And he gives him fifty, half of his value. For now he is worth a hundred, and he may pay half of his value and reduce half of the years.

He gives him a hundred. For he already paid half his value. And if he were not redeeming in parts, the payment of the fifty would not count as a redemption in parts but as an advance, and he would now have to pay him a hundred and fifty, since he is now worth two hundred.

And he became ill and is now worth a hundred, he gives him fifty. For he already redeemed half of the years and now redeems the other half according to his current value. And if he were not redeemed in parts, he would not have to give the fifty, for he had paid him a hundred at the outset, and now he is worth a hundred.
He is not released from his servitude until he writes him a document. For his body is acquired by the master, and therefore waiving the money is no substitute for writing a document.
The slave serves the son until the end of the six. If he was sold by the court (as above, halacha 2).
And one sold to a righteous convert... even the son does not receive his service. Even if the son was born after the conversion (Kesef Mishneh).
It is a mitzvah to say to him "go out" at the time of his leaving. When he goes out at the end of the years (see Mechilta of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, Exodus 21:2).

And even though if he does not say it to him he goes out free and does not need a document. Ideally one should say "go out" to him, but even if he did not say it, he goes out on his own and need not pay anything and need not receive a release document.

Even if he fell ill and his master incurred expenses for him, he owes him nothing. Even if his master did not receive fair return on his purchase and even lost out, the slave need not pay anything upon leaving.
The master is obligated to support his married wife. For the slave has no earnings with which to support his family.

Not a betrothed woman or a woman awaiting yibum. He is not obligated to support a woman who was betrothed to the slave and has not yet entered the wedding canopy, or a woman widowed from his brother who is waiting for the slave to perform yibum with her.
But if she was among those forbidden by a prohibition. A woman forbidden to the slave by a negative commandment.
Even a sheniyah. Sheniyot le'arayot are relatives forbidden by rabbinic enactment (for the list see Hilchot Ishut 1:6).
A woman fit to remain with him. Whom they are permitted to remain married to.

"And his wife shall go out with him" etc.. The Torah says that at the time of release his wife also goes out with him, and certainly this does not mean that during servitude she is enslaved, but that during the servitude she is under the master's authority in the sense that he is obligated to support her.

Regarding one who sells himself it says, "he shall go out from you, he and his children with him," and regarding one sold to a gentile it says etc.. From this it follows that the master is obligated also to support the slave's children, and not only when the court sold him but even when he sold himself and even when he was sold to a gentile (and although regarding one sold by the court only his wife is mentioned and regarding one who sold himself and one sold to a gentile only his children are mentioned, nevertheless we learn from one to the other that in all of them he is obligated to support his wife and children).
Both wife and children etc.. Their law is the same.
A wife and children he had after his sale. That he married a wife or fathered children while he was a slave.
And provided that he took her with the master's consent. That he married the woman with the master's agreement.
He has nothing in the work of their hands. He does not take the profit from their labor.
And in whatever way a husband acquires rights in his wife. See Hilchot Ishut 12:1-4.
His master may give him a Canaanite maidservant. The master is permitted to marry him to a Canaanite maidservant.
As it says, "if his master gives him a wife" etc.. And the continuation of the verse: "the wife and her children shall belong to her master," so it is speaking of a Canaanite maidservant.
He is forbidden with a Canaanite maidservant like the rest of Israel. See Hilchot Issurei Biah 12:11.
And this matter is a received tradition. A tradition of the Sages.

Even if the one sold was a kohen. Who is more stringently treated than an Israelite regarding relations with a gentile woman, since he is forbidden to a zonah by Torah law (see Hilchot Issurei Biah 12:2-3).
As he gives to Canaanites. One Canaanite maidservant to two Canaanite slaves (Hilchot Issurei Biah 14:19).
Pierced. A slave sold by the court who wished to remain more than six years, whose master pierces his ear, as below, halacha 9.
He urges him to leave... and struck him. He urges him to go out, and in doing so struck him to force him to be freed and return to his home.

Exempt, for he became forbidden to the maidservant. Once the Jubilee year arrived the slave is like all of Israel, who are forbidden to a Canaanite maidservant, and since his master struck him to separate him from the prohibition, he is exempt from paying for the injury.
From tradition. The tradition of the Sages in interpreting the verses.
"Forever" - to the "forever" of the Jubilee. The word "forever" in the verse is not meant as eternity but means for the period of the Jubilee, which is a period of many years.
Because he became blemished. And he will not be able to serve in the Temple (Hilchot Biat HaMikdash 6:1, 7:3).

"And he shall return to his family" - to the presumption he had in it. With regard to the status he held by virtue of his family lineage, such as his fitness to serve in the Temple by virtue of being born a kohen.

And he does not return to the position of authority he had. To a public office he held before he was sold, since having been in such a low status he is not fit to be in a position of authority (Meiri, Makkot 13a, Aruch HaShulchan, Yoreh De'ah 267:158).
And states his words before them. The slave says: "I love my master... I will not go free" (Exodus 21:5).
At the end of the six. At the end of the sixth year of his servitude (see below, halacha 10).
The doorpost. One of the posts at the sides of the entrance on which the lintel rests.
When they are standing in a building. Attached and fixed to a structure standing in place.
At the height of an ear. The thick, hard part of the ear.
Until it reaches the door, as it says, "and you shall put it through his ear and into the door". So that the awl passes through the ear and touches the door.

And it does not say doorpost etc.. In Exodus (21:6) it says, "and he shall bring him to the door or to the doorpost," and from this we learn that the slave may stand near the door or near the doorpost and both are not needed, and we also learn that the door must be fixed in its place like a doorpost, and one does not pierce at a detached door.

For one does not perform mitzvot in bundles. One must perform each mitzvah by itself, and not perform several mitzvot together in one bundle, because it appears as if one wants to be rid of the mitzvot (for this principle see also Hilchot Tum'at Tzara'at 11:6, Hilchot Rotzeach 10:5).
That he say it and repeat it. That he say it twice.

Until he says it and repeats it at the end of six, from the start of the last perutah. Both statements must be close to the time of his leaving, so that it will be evident that the words are said with full intent (Meiri, Kiddushin 22a, who wrote that the end of the six means the last day of the sixth year).
For example, when there remains of the day the equivalent of a perutah of his sale price or a little more. The work time remaining until the end of the six years is worth a perutah or a little more.

If the slave had a wife, a Canaanite maidservant etc.. Even if the slave has a wife and children, he is not pierced unless his master also has a wife and children, for both must have a wife and children.
"Because he loves you and your house". You (the master) and your family.
As it says, "because it is good for him with you". That the good is mutual and shared by both.
One who sold himself is sold for six and more than six etc.. Above 2:2-3.
If the court sold him, they give him a parting gift. When he goes out to freedom, his master gives him gifts, as detailed in the following halachot.
One who sold himself is not pierced etc.. Above, halacha 6.
One who sold himself is forbidden to a Canaanite maidservant etc.. Above, halacha 3.
One who sold himself is sold to a gentile etc.. Above 1:3.
And so it appears from the matter of the verse. From the plain meaning of the text.

And what is this that it says, "and also to your maidservant you shall do likewise". Although the beginning of the verse says, "and you shall take the awl and put it through his ear and into the door," the continuation "and also to your maidservant you shall do likewise" is not interpreted as referring to the law of piercing mentioned at the beginning of the verse, but to the law of the parting gift mentioned in the preceding verses.

And Scripture converted it to a positive commandment. A negative prohibition ("you shall not send him away empty") was shifted into a positive commandment ("you shall surely supply him"), and one is not flogged for such a negative commandment (Hilchot Sanhedrin 18:2).
With signs. The growth of two hairs after age twelve; see below 4:1.
Those who go out through the deduction of money. Above 2:8.
Like the matter of flock, threshing floor and winepress etc.. One must give him things similar to flock, grain and wine, which grow and multiply by themselves.
Like the thirty of the slave's fine. That the owner of an ox that gored a slave and killed him pays (Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 11:1).

As it says regarding it, "he shall give to his master". And from this they learned by analogy that this is the measure of giving for the parting gift, regarding which too the language of giving was used ("you shall give him"; Bavli Kiddushin 17a).
"All according to the blessing give to him". That if the master had abundant blessing he should add to him beyond the fixed measure.
And the Jubilee met him while he was fleeing and he went out to freedom. As above 2:4.

And the parting gift of a Hebrew maidservant, and likewise her lost-and-found items, belong to her father. Since she is a na'arah she is still under her father's authority for several matters, and he acquires these things (see Hilchot Ishut 3:11, Hilchot Gezelah VaAvedah 17:13).
The minor. Up to age twelve.
And once she brings two hairs. Once two hairs have grown at her pubic area (see Hilchot Ishut 2:1).
For he still has authority over her etc.. During the period of na'arut, which lasts six months (see ibid. 2:2, 3:11).
Ailonit. A woman whose sexual development is defective, who is unable to bear children and lacks the signs of na'arut (see Hilchot Ishut 2:5).
Her father may sell her. He is permitted to sell her.
The tumtum. One whose sexual organs are covered and it is not known whether he is male or female.
And the androginos. A person with both male and female signs, who is considered a doubtful male, doubtful female.
Not like the law of a Hebrew slave. Perhaps he is a female, who is not sold for theft and does not sell herself (see above 1:2).
And not like the law of a Hebrew maidservant. Perhaps he is a male.

And nevertheless we compel the father to redeem her after he sold her, because of family disgrace. Even if he was forced to sell her, if afterwards he has the means we compel him to redeem her, because it is a disgrace to the family that one of its daughters is a maidservant.
Because he must buy her at a price suited for the deduction etc.. At an amount that allows her to give her portion to redeem herself early, and a perutah is the smallest monetary measure.
She works six years like a slave sold by the court etc.. Above 2:2.

And if the master died, even if he left a son, she goes out free like one who was pierced. Above 3:6-7 (unlike a regular slave, who does not go out upon the father's death if he left a son, as above 2:12).
And if he wrote her a release document and waived the remainder, she goes out free like the slave. Above 2:11.
Who brought signs. Two hairs, as above, halacha 1.
After the day he bought her. A day after he acquired her.
And she returns to her father's authority until she becomes an adult. Until she becomes an adult after six months of na'arut (Hilchot Ishut 2:2).

For she has no days of na'arut but leaves her minority for adulthood. For she is considered a minor until age twenty, and afterwards is considered an adult if she has the signs of an ailonit, and if she has none, she is considered an adult when she is thirty-five (see Hilchot Ishut 2:3-5).
A Hebrew maidservant does not go out through loss of the main limbs. Unlike a Canaanite slave whom his master struck in one of his main limbs, who thereby goes out to freedom (below 5:4).
As we explained in Hilchot Chovel. 4:10.
She is like other betrothed women. See below, halacha 9.
And the mitzvah of designation precedes the mitzvah of redemption. For it is preferable to take her as a wife than to redeem her.
He says to her before two. Two witnesses as in betrothal (Hilchot Ishut 3:1).
For the first money. That he gave in buying her as a maidservant.

The conduct of marriage, not the conduct of servitude. He is obligated in everything a husband owes his wife (see ibid. 12:2), and she performs household tasks as a wife (see ibid. 21:1-7) and not as a maidservant.

If his son was grown etc.. Designation must be done with the consent of the man who betroths, and therefore the father can designate her only for his grown son, and after the son appointed him an agent for this (Bavli Kiddushin 19a).
Even though her father already received her money. And a father may betroth his daughter without her consent (Hilchot Ishut 3:11).
For she went out to freedom at the master's death. As above, halacha 4.
He does not become impure for her. If he is a kohen.

He does not become impure for her, nor inherit her, nor annul her vows until she enters the wedding canopy. For these things pertain to a husband only after marriage (see Hilchot Evel 2:7, Hilchot Ishut 22:1-2, Hilchot Nedarim 11:8).
As we explained. Above, halacha 5.
And not give her to another man. As a gift.

"To a foreign people he shall have no power to sell her, since he dealt treacherously with her". If the master does not designate his maidservant, this constitutes betrayal of her, since she came to his house on the assumption that she would be married to him or his son, which is the preferred mitzvah (above, halacha 7), and if he did not do so he may not sell her to a stranger.

For Scripture needed to forbid this regarding a maidservant only because he may designate her for his son. Since he is permitted to designate her for his son, the Torah wrote explicitly that he may not give her to another man. But a Hebrew slave obviously may not be given away.
Only to one to whom she can be betrothed, either him or his son. To a person to whom she can be betrothed or to his son, such that the betrothal would take effect.
A person may sell his daughter to his father. If the father has a son.
For the master cannot designate her for him. Because she is his granddaughter.
A person may. He is permitted.

For even though they are under a prohibition, betrothal takes effect on them. Even though she is forbidden to marry him, nevertheless if he betrothed her the betrothal takes effect (this speaks of a widow, divorcee and chalutzah whose betrothals were not made by her father but by designation; for if she was betrothed by her father he may not sell her after she was widowed or divorced, as explained in the next halacha).
She fell to a yavam from designation. After she was designated her husband died, and she fell to his brother for yibum.
The chalitzah is invalid because she is a minor. See Hilchot Yibum VeChalitzah 4:16.
She is disqualified from the priesthood. See ibid. 4:26.
As was explained. Above, halacha 12.
And she went out through the years. After six years.
As we explained. Above, halacha 13, that he may sell her to maidservants after maidservants.
And afterwards he went and betrothed her to another. The father betrothed his daughter to another man while she was a maidservant.

If the master wished to designate, he designates etc.. If the master wishes to designate her for himself or his son, the betrothal takes effect, and the betrothal that her father made does not take effect, because the master gave money when he bought her on condition that if he wished to designate her, she would be betrothed retroactively from the time of purchase; so if he wants to designate, the designation betrothal takes precedence. And if he does not want to designate, the betrothal her father made, which was pending, takes effect retroactively when she leaves the master's authority (Bavli Kiddushin 19b).
And stipulated with the master. Made a condition with him.
For he stipulated against what is written in the Torah. For a person cannot exempt himself from what the Torah obligates him (see Hilchot Ishut 6:9).
Canaanite slave. A gentile slave.
Is acquired. From his previous owners to his new master, and if he was previously free he is now acquired by his owner and becomes a slave (see below 9:2).
And acquires himself. To go out to freedom.
By pulling. In a way that he pulled him by force (Hilchot Mechirah 2:3).
And a minor slave. Who has no understanding.
And is acquired by pulling like the pulling of an animal. And therefore it suffices to cause him to walk by calling him or the like (ibid. 3:4).
And we already explained at the beginning of this book. Ibid. 2:1-4, 5:5.
For it is a benefit to him. To be freed from servitude.
And one may act for a person's benefit in his absence. Various acquisitions and the like that are for a person's benefit and advantage are done for him without his knowledge.

And said to him, "on condition that you go out to freedom with it". But if he did not say so to him, the master acquires this money, for the slave's hand is like his master's hand, and the master immediately acquired it (Hilchot Zechiyah UMatanah 3:12-14).
And money or the equivalent of money is the same. They have the same law.
Whether to acquire him or to transfer himself to him. Whether to acquire himself when he goes out to freedom or to transfer himself to the slave.
On paper or on a potsherd. One may write even on these materials.
For this is the body of the release document. The essence of the release document.
And hands him the document before two witnesses. Like a woman's get, which must be handed to her before two witnesses (Hilchot Gerushin 1:13).
Or witnesses were signed on it and he handed it to him privately. Just as a woman's get that has two witnesses signed on it is valid even without witnesses to the delivery (ibid. halacha 16).

For his document and his hand come together. Although the slave's hand is like his master's hand and he cannot acquire anything, he goes out to freedom by receiving the get, because the get separates and releases him from servitude to his master, and at the time of receiving the get his hand becomes independent and he can acquire for himself.
That witnesses testified about him in court. Witnesses testified in the court that he said so.
And even though he made a kinyan from him. That the master made a kinyan sudar on his release (see Hilchot Mechirah 5:5).

He has not yet been freed. For this statement does not have the validity of a release document. However, in cases where the master said things implying that he had resolved in his heart to free him and not retract, we compel him to write a release document (below 8:17, and see Bnei David).

And one who writes to his maidservant, "you are permitted to anyone," has said nothing. For this is not the language of freeing a maidservant but the language of divorcing a wife (see Hilchot Gerushin 1:4).
Why does the Torah mention only tooth and eye?. For only regarding these organs is it specified that the slave goes out to freedom by being struck in them (Exodus 21:26-27).
Blemishes in exposed places. In a visible place on the body.
And they do not return. They do not heal.

Slaves who were circumcised and immersed, for they are partially obligated in mitzvot. One who buys a slave from the gentiles must circumcise him and immerse him for the sake of slavery, and he accepts upon himself the observance of mitzvot (see Hilchot Issurei Biah 13:11, 14:9), and he is obligated in mitzvot like a woman (Hilchot Chagigah 2:1). Such a slave is in an intermediate state, having left the category of gentiles without entering the category of Israel (Hilchot Issurei Biah 12:11), and when he is freed he must immerse again, and thereby he becomes a complete Israelite (ibid. 13:12), and his law is that of a convert (ibid. 14:19).
A slave who is in his gentile state. Who does not wish to be circumcised and accept the mitzvot of slaves but to remain a gentile (see below 8:12).
The tops of the ears. The whole rim of the ear.
And the head of the member. The head of the male organ.
And the tips of the breasts of a woman. The nipples.
He had an extra finger. A slave who has twenty-one fingers.
If it is counted on the back of the hand. That it is in the same row as the other fingers, in which case it is considered an additional limb in its own right (compare Hilchot Tum'at Met 2:7).
His eye was dim. He cannot see with it.
And he gouged it out. He removed it from the body.
He struck opposite his eye and he cannot see etc.. He struck near his eye or ear without touching his body, and as a result he became blind or deaf.
The slave does not go out to freedom through them. For in these cases the blow itself did not cause the blindness or deafness, but he caused it to himself through fear (see Bavli Bava Kamma 91a).
And diminished its light. Impaired his eyesight.
Loose. Wobbling.
If he had already used them to some extent. If before the blow he used the wobbly tooth or weak eye a little.
And his hand dried up. It withered and became paralyzed.
He pulled his beard and loosened a bone of the jaw. He pulled his beard and caused a fracture of the lower jaw.
That he threw a stone at an animal and it fell on the slave. He intended to hit the animal and hit the slave.
He put his hand into his maidservant's womb. To help her in childbirth.
And he said to him, "paint my eye". The slave asked his master to apply ointment to his eye.
"Bore my tooth". He asked him to drill in his aching tooth.
He tricked the master and went out to freedom. He succeeded in deceiving him and causing him to free him.

He goes out to freedom through his tooth and he gives him the value of his eye. For after he knocked out his tooth he is no longer his slave, and the injury to the eye carries the law of payments like any one who injures his fellow (and we do not say that he goes out free through both together and therefore has no payments at all). However, regarding actual payment, it is explained in Hilchot Chovel UMazik (4:11) that if the slave did not receive a release document between the blows, he cannot extract the payment from the master, but if he seized the payment he has acquired it and it is not taken from him (see Kesef Mishneh here and Yad Peshutah there in the name of R. Yehoshua HaNagid).
One who is half slave and half free. One who had two partner owners and one of them freed him, or whose owner freed half of him (see below 7:4).

Because he is not exclusive to his master who injured him. He does not belong only to his master who injured him, but is half free or half belongs to another master, and for such a slave the law of going out through tooth and eye does not apply (Bavli Bava Kamma 90a).

Slaves of iron flock go out through the main limbs if the husband diminished them. Slaves whom the wife brought into her husband's possession at the time of marriage and for whom he took responsibility that in case of divorce or widowhood the wife will receive their value as they were worth at the time of marriage (see Hilchot Ishut 16:1); the husband is considered their master with regard to going out through tooth and eye, since as long as they are married the slaves are in his possession.
And slaves of melog. Slaves whom the wife brought in who are in her possession, except that the husband enjoys them ("eats the fruits") as long as they are married (see ibid. 22:7).
Because they are not exclusive to her. They are not in her exclusive ownership, since the husband has a proprietary right in their fruits.
An ordained court. Who were appointed to be judges (see Hilchot Sanhedrin 4:1-3).

Because it is a fine. The slave's going out is not direct payment for the damage the master caused him but a fine that the Torah imposed on the master, and only an ordained court adjudicates fines (see ibid. 5:8).

Exempt; for if he admits on his own he is not obligated to free him without witnesses. The master is exempt from freeing him and does not even have to take a modified oath against the slave's claim, since he denied a monetary claim that even if he had admitted to it he would not be liable (see Hilchot To'en VeNit'an 1:15, Even HaAzel).
As we explained in Hilchot Genevah. 1:5.
And acquired it for him through another. He gave the document to another person to acquire the release on the slave's behalf.

He cannot retract, and the slave does not go out to freedom until the get reaches his hand. Although the master cannot retract after giving the get to the agent, nevertheless the slave is freed only when the get reaches his hands.
They may not give it after death. For the giving of the get into the slave's hand is what frees him, and there is no get after death (Hilchot Gerushin 9:22).
One who writes in a document etc.. And gave it to the slave.
He did not go out to freedom. For this is only a promise that he will make him free in the future (for a similar law see Hilchot Zechiyah UMatanah 4:11).
We are concerned lest he acquired it for him through another. Without the slave's knowledge, as above, halacha 1.

A litigant's admission is like a hundred witnesses. When a person admits that he is obligated it is like a hundred witnesses, and here the slave admits that he was not freed (for a similar law see Hilchot Zechiyah UMatanah 4:12).
This is a maidservant as she was. For he did not use language that indicates release, and therefore the children she bears will be slaves (Kesef Mishneh, based on Bavli Gittin 40a).
And the heirs are forbidden to enslave her. To give her hard labor.
And likewise if he said etc.. See also Hilchot Zechiyah UMatanah 9:12.
All documents that are drawn up in gentile courts. Any document that is confirmed and ratified in the courts of gentiles.
In Hilchot Halva'ah. Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 27:1.

A Cuthean. The Cutheans, called "Samaritans," were exiled from Cutha to the Land of Israel and converted out of fear, and at first were presumed to observe mitzvot, and therefore in some laws their halachic status was the same as that of Jews (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Berachot 8:8).
And provided that the Cuthean is a chaver. Who accepted upon himself to observe mitzvot and be meticulous in them.
For Cutheans are like gentiles in all their matters. Since it became known that they worship idols (Commentary on the Mishnah, ibid.).
To the Sadducees. People who challenge the tradition and authority of the Sages of the Oral Torah (see Hilchot Teshuvah 3:8, Hilchot Mamrim 3:3).
And wrote it for her sake. That the writing of the get be done for the sake of the divorce of a particular woman (see Hilchot Gerushin 1:3).

One who lacks only the giving - this excludes one who writes on something attached and afterwards cuts it off. The get must be written in a way that no further act is needed before giving it. Therefore if it was written on something attached to the ground and afterwards cut off and given, the get is invalid (see ibid. halacha 6).
Their witnesses sign only in each other's presence. One in the presence of the other.
In Hilchot Gerushin. 9:29.
He need not say "it was written in my presence and signed in my presence". In order to verify and confirm the document (see Hilchot Gerushin 7:1).
If there are no witnesses to confirm it. If there are no witnesses present to testify to the authenticity of the get.
And if the master came and contested it. Claimed that he did not write the document and it is forged.
As we explained regarding women's gittin. Ibid. 7:5-6.
And she need not confirm it. She need not say "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed" or bring witnesses to testify to its authenticity (see Hilchot Gerushin 7:24).
It came out from under her hand. It was found with her.

If he stipulated with her. The husband did not give her the get to divorce her but in the manner of agency, telling her to carry the get to such-and-such a court and they will give her the get properly.
As we explained in its place. Ibid. halacha 23.
Anyone fit to bring a woman's get. Everyone is fit except a gentile, slave, deaf-mute, mentally incompetent person and minor (Hilchot Gerushin 6:6).
And a slave may receive a get for his fellow from the hand of his fellow's master. One slave may receive a get for a second slave from the hand of the second one's master.

But not from the hand of the receiver's own master. If both are slaves of one master, he cannot receive from the master on behalf of the other slave, since his hand is like his master's hand and so the get is still in the master's possession.
And she is not betrothed. Since she was not freed, for betrothal of a maidservant does not take effect.
A thing that severs between him and his masters. That separates and cuts off.
And no right remains to the master in him. That the content of the get deal entirely with the slave's right and not the master's right.
This is not severing and the get is void. Since the get records a right of the master, that a certain asset remains his, this is not a bill of severance (Kesef Mishneh).
And he did not acquire any of the property. For he was not freed, and the slave's hand is like his master's hand.
Until the get is confirmed through its signatories. Until it is proven that the get is authentic by verifying the signatures (for the methods of confirmation see Hilchot Edut 6:2).
Like other documents. For if the document was not confirmed one cannot collect with it, since one can claim that the signatures were forged.
He acquired himself. For he is included among the property.
For he is trusted to bring his release document and need not confirm it. As above 6:7.
Rather they write a document for each one. To free them, a separate document must be written for each, just as two women are not divorced with one get (see Hilchot Gerushin 4:19).

And they free each other. For the first slave has a share in all the property, which includes the second slave, and the second slave has a share in all the property, which includes the first slave. Therefore they free each other and divide the remaining property.

For the slave is part of the property and he retained half of them. When he wrote that he gives half his property to each of the slaves, he retained in each of the documents half of the slave he did not free, and such a get does not work, since the master retains a right in the slave.
Who took half his value. Who received half of his redemption price (as above 5:2).
In what case is this said?. That half the slave was not freed.
And left his half. He kept half for himself.

He freed half of him and sold half of him, or freed half of him and gave half as a gift. For example, where first he sold or gave half and afterward handed the slave the release document, or did so in a manner that both occurred at once. But if he first freed half and afterward sold or gave half, the buyer did not acquire, because at the time of the release it had not left his ownership completely (Kesef Mishneh).
That one of them freed his portion, whether with money or with a document, acquired half. Because the partner freed everything that was in his possession.

For this is like one who freed half of her. Because the fetus is considered part of its mother's body and follows her. But the mother does not follow the fetus, and therefore one who says "you are free, your offspring is a slave," the offspring does not hold back the mother's release (Lechem Mishneh).

A charufah maidservant. A woman who is half Canaanite maidservant and half free, who was betrothed to a Hebrew slave. Her betrothal is not a complete betrothal because of her maidservant portion, and when she is freed the betrothal is completed and she becomes fully a married woman (see Hilchot Issurei Biah 3:13, Hilchot Ishut 4:16-17, where it is explained that the law is the same if an Israelite who is not a Hebrew slave betrothed her).
For even money completes her release. And not like one who says that she is completely freed only with a document (see Bavli Gittin 39b).
Not with a maidservant. Because of his free portion.
And not with a free woman. Because of his slave portion.
And he writes a document for him for half his value. A promissory note in which the slave obligates himself to pay him for the value of his half.
For a man is commanded to be fruitful and multiply. See Hilchot Ishut 15:2.
And if the sinful treated her as ownerless. Because she cannot marry, she makes herself available for immorality with sinful men (see also below 9:6).

That his master got up and transferred his half to his minor son so that the court would not compel him to free him. The master transferred to his minor son the half of the slave that belongs to him, to avoid the release, since the court does not compel a minor to do anything.

Apotropos. An appointee who will be responsible for the minor's property. [Note: the vocalization of this word follows the Greek original. In the Rambam's own handwriting in the Commentary on the Mishnah, several forms of vocalization of this word appear: sometimes the first pe is vocalized with a kubutz, sometimes with a patach (and in some places the pe is unvocalized).]
And if the minor became attached to the slave and longs for him. If the minor is drawn to the slave and misses him.
They persuade him to part from him with money. They convince him to separate from the slave by giving him money.
A seriously ill person. A dangerously ill person who is near death.
And he recovered. He recovered from his illness.
He retrieves the property. The transfer is nullified and the property returns to him, for he made the transfer only out of concern that he would die (Hilchot Zechiyah UMatanah 8:14).
For he is already known as a free man. It became publicly known that he is a free man (see also ibid. halacha 22).

And we compel his master to go back and buy him etc.. The Sages fined the seller to buy the slave back from the gentile even at ten times his true price, and then to free him. For the sale of a Canaanite slave to a gentile removes him from the fulfillment of the mitzvot he is obligated in (as he becomes subject to the gentile's labor), and the Sages did not want a Jew to sell his slave to a gentile (Bavli Gittin 43b-44a and Rashi there).
An expert court. Of ordained judges (Hilchot Sanhedrin 5:8, and see above 5:17).
He borrowed against his slave from a gentile. He borrowed money from the gentile and obligated himself that if he did not repay the money he would give him the slave in payment of the debt.
That he acquire the body of this slave. That the gentile lender receive the slave himself in exchange for the debt.
He goes out to freedom immediately. At the time of the loan, like the law of one who sells his slave, for borrowing against the body of his slave too is included in the fine the Sages imposed.
That he acquire the work of his hands. That he receive the product the slave makes through his labor.
The gentile collected him for his debt. In a case where the Israelite did not borrow against his slave, but the gentile himself decided to take the slave on account of the debt.
Or from his nobles. The ministers of the king.
Even though he fears them. And out of fear was compelled to sell to him.
He sold him to a gentile for thirty days. A sale for a fixed time.

He sold him except for his labor. That he sold him so that the buyer could marry him to his maidservant and have offspring from him, while he still does all the work for the seller; in this case he has not removed him from the mitzvot (Rashi, Gittin 44a).
Except for the mitzvot. On condition that he can continue to observe mitzvot.
If the slave seized the equivalent of his value etc.. If the slave seized from his master's property an amount with which he can free himself from the gentile, it is not taken from him.
To a resident alien. A gentile who accepted the Noahide commandments because of God's command and wants to live in the Land of Israel (Hilchot Issurei Biah 14:7, Hilchot Melachim 8:11).
To a Cuthean. See above 6:6 in the commentary.
To an apostate Israelite. A Jew who converted out of his religion.
One who sells his slave outside the Land. To another Israelite living outside the Land.
He goes out free. A rabbinic fine because he took him out of the Land (Rashi, Gittin 43b).
And the money is lost. The buyer loses the money he paid for him.

To Syria. Places north of the Land of Israel, in the region still called Syria today, which, since King David conquered them before completing the conquest of the Land of Israel, are not considered fully the Land of Israel (Hilchot Terumot 1:3).
And even to Acco. Which was not conquered by those who ascended from Babylonia, and for several purposes is considered outside the Land (ibid. halacha 9).

And brought in slaves and maidservants for him. She brought them from her father's house, and as long as they are married the proceeds of their labor ("fruits") belong to the husband, and the slaves themselves ("the body") belong to the wife.
A slave who went out after his master to Syria. Of his own will, since his master cannot compel him to go outside the Land (as below, halacha 9).
He lost his right. And he does not go out to freedom.
A slave who said to go up to the Land of Israel. A slave of an Israelite living outside the Land who wishes to go up to the Land of Israel.
We compel his master to go up with him. For a similar law regarding a married man and woman see Hilchot Ishut 13:19-20.
The master wished to leave for outside the Land. If he was living in the Land and wished to leave for outside the Land.

And even in this time when the Land is in the hands of gentiles. For it is preferable to live in the Land of Israel in a city most of whose inhabitants are gentiles than to live outside the Land in a city most of whose inhabitants are Israelites (Hilchot Melachim 5:12).
And he shall write a promissory note for his value until he gets the means and gives it to him. The slave will obligate himself by document to repay his value to the master when he obtains money.
He is a righteous convert. For a Canaanite slave after his release is a convert after he immerses (Hilchot Issurei Biah 13:2).
And Scripture added another warning for one who counts him. One who causes him distress with words transgresses an additional prohibition besides the prohibitions that apply to every convert.

He transgresses three negative commandments. Three prohibitions that pertain to verbal wronging (unlike an ordinary convert, regarding whom there are two prohibitions against verbal wronging), and another additional prohibition stated in the language of monetary wronging as with every convert, as below.
Because of "you shall not wrong one another". The prohibition against distressing any Israelite with words.
And because of "you shall not wrong a convert". An additional prohibition specific to distressing a convert.

And likewise he transgresses "and you shall not oppress him," as we explained regarding wronging. In Hilchot Mechirah 14:15-17 it is explained that one who torments a convert with words also transgresses the prohibition stated regarding monetary wronging (although there it cited the verse said regarding monetary wronging of an Israelite and here it cited the verse said regarding monetary wronging of a convert; see Even HaAzel there who explained this).

And did not wish to be circumcised and accept the mitzvot of slaves. For so is the law of a Canaanite slave, who must be circumcised and immerse and then he is obligated in mitzvot like a woman (see above 5:5 in the commentary).
They roll with him. They try to persuade him to agree to be circumcised and accept the mitzvot.
And if the slave stipulated with him at the outset. If the slave made a condition with the buyer in advance.

He is permitted to keep him as long as he wants to remain in his gentile state. But he must accept upon himself to observe the seven Noahide commandments and he becomes a resident alien (see also Hilchot Milah 1:6, Hilchot Issurei Biah 14:9).
He threw himself to the troops. He fled from his master's house and presented himself to be taken as a soldier in the army.

It is permitted for him to take his price from the gentiles and to write and register it in their courts. He is permitted to receive money from the gentiles and to write a bill of sale and to give it validity in a gentile court, even though it is like selling him to them.
Because he is like one who rescues from their hands. He extracts from them money that he would otherwise lose.
And he needs a release document. To complete his conversion process and to permit him to marry an Israelite woman.
Whoever redeems him as a slave. Another person who redeemed him in order to enslave him.
Takes his redemption money from his master. Takes from the master the money he paid to redeem him.

And if he redeemed him as a free man, he returns to his first master for nothing. For the redeemer cannot free the slave since the master did not despair of him, and the master need not pay him for the redemption since he did not redeem on his behalf.
A slave whom his master made a lien for his creditor. He designated him for collection of the debt.

He is freed. Even though he pledged the slave to the lender. And even if he told the lender that he could collect the debt only from the slave, he goes out to freedom and the borrower must pay the lender the debt (see Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 18:6).

A slave whose master married him to a free woman. An Israelite woman who is forbidden to a slave; it can be assumed that he did not intend to marry him in transgression but intended to free him before the marriage.
For only a free man is obligated in them. And they do not apply to a Canaanite slave because he is not a complete Israelite (see Hilchot Issurei Biah 12:11; 12:17).
He goes out to freedom. For by these acts the master revealed his intention that he frees him.

He vowed a vow that slaves are compelled regarding. For example, a nazirite vow, which the master compels him to violate, for vows involving affliction of the soul and the like do not take effect on him at all and there is no need to compel him regarding them.
As we explained regarding vows. Hilchot Nezirut 2:17-18.
He goes out to freedom. And after his release he must complete the nazirite period he accepted upon himself.

For since he did not compel him... he revealed his intention that he released his servitude. For the way to annul a slave's vow is by compulsion and not by nullification, and since he did to him an act that is done to a free man, he shows thereby that he freed him.

That he made him an apotropos. He honored him and gave him responsibility over his property or children. Even so this is not conclusive proof that he frees him, for sometimes he relies greatly on the slave's trustworthiness and makes him an apotropos.
And did not object to him, he does not go out to freedom. For it is possible that he did not feel a need to object, and this is no proof that he frees him.
And if he taught him, he does not go out to freedom. For it is possible that he taught him Torah so that he would know to be careful with prohibitions (Even HaAzel).

And the slave went ahead and immersed in front of his master for the sake of a free man. A Canaanite slave acquired by an Israelite must immerse for the sake of slavery, which is like a partial conversion. But this slave intended at the time of the immersion that he was immersing for the sake of complete conversion.

He goes out to freedom. Since his master was present there and did not announce that the immersion was for slavery, the slave's intention is effective for a conversion immersion (see also Hilchot Issurei Biah 13:11).

And not in the presence of his master, he must specify. When the slave immerses while his master is not present, his intention for conversion is ineffective; rather, if he wishes to convert he must say explicitly to the judges, "I am immersing before you for the sake of conversion."

Therefore his master must restrain him in the water. So that the slave will not intend conversion and become free, his master must grip him firmly while he is in the water so that he not leave his control until he comes up from there, and state to the judges that he is immersing him for slavery (ibid.).
Who seized a minor gentile. Took hold by force of a gentile child.

For the sake of a convert, he is a convert. Just as a minor can be converted by the court's decision (Hilchot Issurei Biah 13:7), and he becomes a convert provided he did not protest when he grew up (Hilchot Melachim 10:3).

For the sake of a free man. If he was previously a slave of a gentile (Even HaAzel). Some rule the halacha differently and explain that the words "and immersed him for the sake of a convert, he is a convert" are a kind of heading, followed by two options of immersion for the sake of a convert: one option for the sake of a slave, which is partial conversion, and a second for the sake of a free man, which is complete conversion (R. Y. Kafih).

a convert whose maidservants preceded him etc.. A gentile who came to convert, and before he immersed for conversion his slaves went ahead and immersed in his presence, are free (and it does not help if he forces them into the water, since he is still a gentile - Or Sameach).
an Israelite who had relations with a Canaanite maidservant. In violation of the prohibition, since it is forbidden to have relations with her as a gentile (Hilchot Issurei Biah 12:11).
even though she is his maidservant. And we do not say that presumably he freed her before he had relations with her (see Hilchot Gerushin 10:19).
the child is a Canaanite slave for all purposes. For a child born to a Canaanite maidservant follows her (Hilchot Issurei Biah 15:4).
whether one acquires a Canaanite slave etc.. It makes no difference whether he acquires the slave from an Israelite or from a resident alien, etc.
a gentile who is subjugated under our hand. Subject to Israelite rule.
he is a Canaanite slave for all purposes. All the laws of a Canaanite slave apply to him.

for it says: "that they begot in your land," and a slave has no lineage. The relationship between a slave and his offspring has no legal significance, and so it cannot be said of a slave "that they begot."
one of the nations who came etc.. See also Hilchot Issurei Biah 15:6.

as it says: "that they begot in your land". The verse is interpreted as referring to those begotten of a woman who is the Canaanite maidservant of an Israelite (the word "in your land" is interpreted as "in your possession").
but a slave of ours who had relations with one of the nations. A Canaanite slave of an Israelite who had relations with a gentile woman who is not a maidservant.

and likewise if their law was that whoever does not pay the tax is sold. Or that he is enslaved to whoever paid the fine on his behalf (Hilchot Gezelah 5:16; see there that if one paid the fine for a poor Israelite, he may enslave him but may not work him as a slave).
their law is law. For the conditions in which the king's law applies, see there, halachot 14 and 18.
his body is acquired by the Israelite. After he immerses him for the purpose of slavery (Kesef Mishneh, and see above 8:19).
because of suspicion. Lest she commit adultery with him.
a slave of nine years and from nine years upward. The age fit for intercourse (Hilchot Issurei Biah 1:13-14).
and if he freed him, he is freed, as we have explained. Above 5:1-3, that a slave can acquire himself with money or with a document.

and they compel him to write a deed of release in all the ways we have explained. In all cases where the master freed his slave without a deed of release, the slave goes free and the master is compelled to write him a deed of release (above 8:13-17).
as a mitzvah of their words. A mitzvah of the Sages.
a maidservant whom the people treated as ownerless. See also above 7:7.
work for me and I will not feed you. Work, and I will not give you sustenance.
for Israelites are commanded to keep slaves among them alive. And surely they will give him sustenance.

for the court does not intervene to guard the property of adults. The court does not take responsibility for guarding the property of an adult, since he is responsible for it himself, and providing a slave with sustenance is part of guarding one's own property.

in the manner of nikhsei melog property. Nikhsei melog is property that the wife brought with her from her father's house, for whose value the husband did not take responsibility; after divorce or widowhood the property returns to her as it is, and if it diminished or was lost the husband need not pay her for it (Hilchot Ishut 16:1).
he is obligated to feed them, by the court. The court obligates him to give them sustenance (see also there 22:25).
for she brought them in on this condition. On the understanding that the husband would not be negligent in guarding them and caring for them.
it is permitted to work a Canaanite slave with rigor. Unlike a Hebrew slave (see above 1:6).

Did not He who made me in the belly make him, and did one fashion us in the womb?. He who made me in my mother's belly also made my slave in his mother's belly, for the one God formed us both in the womb.
they are compassionate toward all. See also Hilchot Issurei Biah 19:17, Hilchot Matnot Aniyim 10:2.
for He commanded us to emulate them. See Hilchot De'ot 1:6.
